title: Rijksmuseum uses neural networks to reconstruct the strips cut from Rembrandt's The Night Watch in 1715
summary: Rijksmuseum used neural networks to reconstruct The Night Watch's 1715-trimmed edges, displayed complete from 23 June 2021.
account: On 23 June 2021 the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam put Rembrandt's The Night Watch on display with reconstructions of the strips cut from all four sides in 1715, when the canvas was trimmed to fit a wall in the Town Hall. Rijksmuseum senior scientist Robert Erdmann trained artificial neural networks on the original and on a seventeenth-century copy attributed to Gerrit Lundens to generate the missing sections in Rembrandt's style; the printed reconstructions were mounted around the original for the following months. Director Taco Dibbits said: 'Thanks to this reconstruction, we can now see that the composition as it was painted by Rembrandt was even more dynamic.' Hyperallergic reported the project independently on 24 June 2021.
purpose: The networks were built specifically to reconstruct the trimmed sections from the Lundens copy; the display was that purpose.
system: Artificial neural networks trained on The Night Watch and the Lundens copy (Rijksmuseum, Robert Erdmann)
taxonomy_note: Could also be read as Improved Accessibility (public access to the full composition); Knowledge Discovery chosen because the reconstruction revealed the composition as originally painted.

ratings.reason: Visitors could see the composition complete for the first time in 300 years; a cultural benefit from a temporary display.
The museum gained a research-based reconstruction and a public exhibition.

ai_role.statement: The neural networks generated the pixel content of the missing strips in Rembrandt's style from the Lundens copy; the copy's existence and curatorial choices were preconditions.
